title: Shortest paths in Python (heapq, deque, inf)
seriesDescription: Shortest paths, union-find, tries, intervals, bits, dynamic programming, greedy and backtracking with Python code. JEE-Advanced style: integer, assertion-reason, matrix match, fill-in-the-blanks, short code and multi-correct questions.
description: Dijkstra with heapq and lazy deletion, tuple tie-breaking pitfalls, 0-1 BFS with deque, Bellman-Ford for K stops and Floyd-Warshall on list-of-lists tables.
source: Python heapq and collections.deque docs; CLRS ch. 22-24; cp-algorithms; LeetCode Cheapest Flights Within K Stops, Network Delay Time

questions.prompt: Write a Python function `dijkstra(g, src)` where g[u] is a list of `(v, weight)` pairs with non-negative weights. Return the list of shortest distances from src (`float('inf')` for unreachable nodes) using `heapq`.
questions.explanation: This is the lazy-deletion version: `heapq` has no decrease-key, so duplicates are pushed and stale ones skipped. Other correct variants (a `visited` set, a `dict` for `dist`) pass the intent. Time O(E log V). `float('inf')` needs no overflow care because Python floats saturate at infinity.

checks.label: uses heapq push and pop on (distance, node) tuples
initialises dist to infinity and dist[src] to 0
relaxes an edge when d + w improves dist[v]

questions.prompt: Write a Python function `cheapest(n, flights, src, dst, k)` where flights is a list of `(u, v, w)`. Return the cheapest price using at most k stops, or -1 if impossible. Use Bellman-Ford rounds.
questions.explanation: The copy matters: relaxing in place could chain several edges in one round and exceed the K-stop limit. Time O(K * E). A BFS/heap solution tracking (cost, node, stops) is another valid approach, but it would not satisfy these Bellman-Ford checks.

relaxes from a copy of the previous round
relaxes each edge with dist[u] + w

questions.prompt: Write a Python function `floyd(dist)` that updates an n x n matrix in place to all-pairs shortest distances (`float('inf')` where no edge, 0 on the diagonal) and returns it.
questions.explanation: O(n^3) time, O(1) extra space. The intermediate vertex k must be the outer loop. It suits small dense graphs (n up to a few hundred); for sparse large graphs run Dijkstra from each source.

checks.label: tests a path through the middle vertex

questions.prompt: Directed edges A->B 4, A->C 1, C->B 2, C->D 8, B->D 5, D->E 3. Dijkstra from A uses `heapq` with lazy deletion: one `heappush` for the source, then one per successful relaxation. How many times is `heappush` called in total?
questions.explanation: Source (1), A relaxes B and C (3), C relaxes B to 3 and D to 9 (5), B relaxes D to 8 (6), D relaxes E (7). The stale entries (4, B) and (9, D) are popped and skipped. In general pushes are at most E + 1.

questions.prompt: Heap entries are tuples `(distance, node)`, where node is an instance of a plain class that defines no ordering methods. What can happen when two entries have the same distance?
questions.explanation: Fix: use integer node ids, or push `(distance, counter, node)` with a unique counter as tie-breaker, the pattern in the `heapq` documentation.

options.text: Comparison moves on to the node objects and raises `TypeError`.
options.why: Correct: tuples compare element by element, so equal first items force a comparison of the second.

options.text: The heap silently keeps the insertion order for entries with equal distances.
options.why: `heapq` is not stable and never records insertion order by itself.

options.text: `heapq` sorts by the first tuple element only and ignores the rest.
options.why: Tuples compare lexicographically; later elements are used whenever earlier ones tie.

options.text: Entries with equal distances are merged into one entry to save memory.
options.why: A heap never merges entries; both stay as separate items.

questions.prompt: True or false: `heapq` provides a decrease-key operation, so Dijkstra can update an existing entry in place.
questions.explanation: Removing an arbitrary item from the list is O(n) and breaks the heap invariant until re-heapified. Lazy deletion is the standard approach.

options.why: `heapq` only offers `push`, `pop`, `pushpop`, `replace` and `heapify` on a plain list.
Correct: there is no decrease-key; stale entries are skipped after popping.

questions.prompt: Complete the Python container choice for 0-1 BFS.
questions.explanation: `collections.deque` has O(1) operations at both ends (a list's `insert(0, x)` is O(n)). Front insertion for free moves keeps the `deque` ordered by distance, giving O(V + E).
questions.text: 0-1 BFS keeps its frontier in a {1}: a neighbour reached by a weight-0 edge goes in with {2}, one reached by a weight-1 edge goes in with {3}.

questions.prompt: A developer prints a list h after calling `heapq.heappush` on the values 5, 1, 4, 2 in turn.
questions.explanation: To read in order, pop repeatedly or call `sorted(h)`. The list layout is the implicit heap tree, not sorted order.
questions.assertion: Printing or iterating the list h shows the values in ascending order.
questions.reason: `heapq` stores a binary heap in a plain list, which only guarantees that `h[0]` is the smallest item.

whys.a: A is false, so R cannot explain it.
whys.c: A is false, and R is true.
whys.d: Right: R is true and is exactly why A is false; only repeated heappop returns sorted order.

questions.prompt: You need a max-heap of distances using `heapq`.
questions.explanation: Negate numbers, or wrap them in a small class with reversed comparison. `heapq.nlargest` also exists for top-k queries.
questions.assertion: `heapq` is a min-heap only, so a max-heap is built by pushing negated keys.

whys.a: R is false, so it cannot explain A.
whys.c: Right: A is true, but heapify builds the heap bottom-up in O(n), so R is false.

questions.prompt: Consider the cost of `heapq` operations on a heap of n items.
questions.explanation: Both facts feed the Dijkstra bound: up to E pops at O(log V) each.
questions.reason: Reading the smallest item with `h[0]` runs in O(1).

whys.a: Peeking at h[0] being O(1) does not explain why heappop must sift.
whys.b: Right: both are true; heappop must restore the heap by sifting, while h[0] is a plain index, and neither explains the other.

questions.prompt: A student sets `dist = [float('inf')] * n` and relaxes with `dist[u] + w < dist[v]` without checking reachability.
questions.explanation: Integers in Python never overflow either, so a large int sentinel works too; `float('inf')` just compares correctly with every number.
questions.assertion: Using `float('inf')` as the initial distance needs no overflow guard when u is unreachable.
questions.reason: In IEEE 754 floating point, infinity plus a finite number is still infinity.

whys.a: Right: inf + w stays inf, which is never smaller than dist[v], so no bogus distance appears.
whys.b: R is the direct cause of A.

questions.prompt: Match each shortest-path need with the Python construct that fits it.
questions.explanation: `deque` gives O(1) at both ends; `heapq` turns a list into a min-heap; `defaultdict(list)` saves the membership test. A list's `pop(0)` is O(n), so it is a poor queue.

Frontier ordered by distance in Dijkstra

right.text: A list managed with `heapq` push and pop

questions.prompt: After popping `(d, u)` from the heap in lazy-deletion Dijkstra, which check prevents redoing work for outdated entries?
questions.explanation: Without the check the algorithm stays correct but can re-expand a node many times, degrading toward O(V * E) on dense graphs.

options.why: This skips exactly the valid entries and keeps the stale ones.
Correct: a larger d than the recorded best means a better entry was already processed.
Membership on a list is linear and the popped entry is no longer inside.
A popped node always has a finite distance, so this never triggers.
